source.title: Emergent Hierarchical Monosemantic Neurons from the Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward Algorithm
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; Qinglin Qi; Zhao-Qian Yao; Harshvardhan Saini; Dian-Bo Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study proposes and evaluates GCFF-generated visual features, not the claim versions’ audits of a model’s own neurons, neuron-pole shares, attribution graphs, or held-out activation prediction.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for a GCFF interpretation module attached to CLIP-ViT-L/14. These are measurements of selected, newly trained module neurons, not the base model’s own neuron poles or the claim’s specific proportions. The paper also cites a meaningfulness threshold from prior work; that cited result is not recorded as a row.
record.test_reason: The study trains a new GCFF module on frozen CLIP-ViT-L/14 embeddings and scores explanations for its own neurons. It does not measure the base model's own neurons, so none of the claim's targets are covered: pole shares, cross-model shares, the InceptionV1 cases, attribution graphs, or held-out activation simulation. Its quantitative results cover only 430 neurons pre-selected for consistency (top 20 per layer), so they give no share of interpretable neurons. They are scored against the same top-20 activating images used to write the explanations, so they cannot speak to V6 or V7 either. The paper treats polysemanticity of base-model neurons as a background premise and does not test it.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also claim two further things. First, GCFF neurons are non-linear functions of the representation, so they escape the Linear Representation Hypothesis that constrains sparse dictionary learning. Second, GCFF trained from scratch is state of the art among forward-forward algorithms on MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10 and CIFAR-100.
record.recipe_differences: GCFF trains class-routed, multilayer modules with local forward-forward objectives and evaluates selected visual-feature explanations; it is not the neuron-pole audit or held-out activation-scoring procedure described in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Qualitative feature examples vary across module layers and datasets. The reported alignment metrics are aggregated across ImageNet-1K and STL-10, so dataset-specific or layer-specific quantitative sensitivity is not reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons in a trained GCFF interpretation module on CLIP embeddings were selected for consistency and then scored in-sample on their top-20 images. They received high explanation-alignment scores, and the two LLM evaluators agreed closely.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For 430 consistency-selected neurons in a 3-layer GCFF module on CLIP-ViT-L/14 embeddings (ImageNet-1K and STL-10), mean in-sample alignment was 0.829 (GPT-5.4-mini) and 0.824 (Gemini-3-Flash). Evaluator agreement was 91.0% (kappa 0.687).

record.problems: The quantitative neuron evaluation selects the top 20 neurons per layer after screening for internal consistency, and the reported alignment results are aggregated across two datasets. The explanations and judgments concern top-response images; the study does not report held-out activation-prediction tests.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible reported results left out.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles; no one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No language models, no MoE models, no scale comparison.
No analysis of InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or of recursive generalization versus superposition.

No interpretable-neuron share for any model's own neurons. No comparison of architectures or tools on base-model neurons. The GCFF neurons are a trained add-on module, and only screened neurons were scored.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with a replacement model.
Explanations are checked against the same top-20 activating images used to write them. No test of predicting where a neuron fires.
No simulation-based scoring of activations on new inputs.

record.verdict_notes: The 0.5 meaningfulness threshold is cited from Wasserman et al. (2025) and correctly not recorded as a row. The classification accuracies in Table 2 are the study's own method compared with others and bear on no version. The layer-wise hierarchy is supported only by qualitative examples. The relation could arguably be 'assumes', because the paper takes base-model neuron polysemanticity as a premise. Either way the paper does not engage the claim directly.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report proportions with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Does not test the stated shares across language models, dense and MoE architectures, or model scales.
Does not analyze InceptionV1’s cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models or compare the proposed architecture/tools against those estimates.
Does not build attribution graphs from a large model’s own neurons or compare them with a replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations derived from activating examples predict activations on separate examples.
Does not score explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text.
